newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: New Australian wool trading instrument to go ahead.
newsitem.headline: New Australian wool trading instrument to go ahead.

text.p: Australian plans for commercial trading in a new leveraged instrument for wool will go ahead following effective approval by the Federal government, Macquarie Bank Ltd and the Wool Council of Australia said on Wednesday.

Australia's Minister for Primary Industries and Energy John Anderson earlier on Wednesday announced planned amendments to the Wool International Act which will allow wool producers early access to cash benefits on their tax entitlements to wool in Wool International's stockpile.

Macquarie Bank would begin trading wool tax entitlements as soon as legislation was passed following the decision to allow the transfer of entitlements, Randell Heyman, director of the bank's treasury and commodities group, said in a statement.
"Now you don't have to buy a sheep to invest in wool," Peter Walsh, assistant director of grower organisation Wool Council of Australia (WCA), commented to Reuters.

The new leveraged instrument would provide growers with a commercial choice on whether they took their equity in the wool stockpile now or later and gave potential investors a vehicle to make a leveraged play on the wool price outlook, he said.
Return of grower equity in Wool International, holder of Australia's wool stockpile, is to proceed over the next three to four years, WCA president Rod Thirkell-Johnston said.
An interim payment of about A$75 million to A$80 million will be made in late 1997. This will be followed by a payment of about A$250 million in 1998/99.
Distribution of the remaining equity of up to A$500 million will occur in 2000/01 and possibly be spread over the final two years of the stockpile, Thirkell-Johnston said.

A wool producer with an average wool income of A$100,000 a year between 1993/94 and 1995/96, when the wool tax was payable by growers to meet debt on the wool stockpile, could expect an interim payment of about A$3,000, while total equity return was estimated at about A$30,000, he said.
Tradability of equity entitlements in the wool stockpile would enable all eligible wool taxpayers to trade their instruments well before the distribution of funds, he said.
Buyers may include other growers or investors from outside the industry, while the instrument could be used as security for borrowings, he said.
Wool industry dynamics were changing for the better with the steady run-down in the stockpile and withdrawal of the government from the industyry, he said.
WCA had had informal discussion with other merchant banks for their entry into trading of the wool certificates but only Macquarie was so far involved, Walsh said.
Australia's wool stockpile of about 1.8 million bales is down from its peak of almost five million bales in 1991.
Macquarie Bank already has a forward micron indicator wool contract and has so far traded more than 50,000 bales of wool through this over-the-counter instrument.
